title: A Compass for the Harbor
premise: In the winter of 1899, Marguerite Zhou, a battlefield nurse of mixed heritage working a fog-bound harbor hospital, keeps a private ledger recording the names and last words of soldiers that official reports omit. When a dying colonel presses a sealed letter into his hands—one naming the Zhou family in an inheritance conspiracy reaching the colonial governor's office—Marguerite becomes both courier and target, forced to move the evidence past three military checkpoints before New Year's Eve seals the estate's transfer forever. Along the way he gathers an unlikely found family: a disgraced ferry pilot, a widow who runs the harbor tavern, and the orphaned daughter of a soldier in his ledger. At the climax, cornered at the final checkpoint on New Year's Eve, Marguerite chooses to surrender his invisibility entirely, reading the ledger aloud as testimony; the letter reaches its destination, the inheritance is redirected to those the dead actually named, and Marguerite finally claims a place—and a family—at the harbor.
about_author: Quentin Sandoval is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters in colonial port records before turning to fiction. He writes from a house above a working harbor, where he still collects the names strangers leave behind.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In the harbor hospital's fever ward, he records the final words of soldiers that officers' reports erase, hiding the ledger beneath a loose floorboard. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: he measures dignity in what can be carried when orders come, establishing his creed of careful invisibility.

chapters.title: Fog at the Third Pier
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A routine supply run to the piers introduces Ilsa Brandt, the ferry pilot stripped of her license for refusing to carry troops, and the widow Odile who runs the tavern. Marguerite observes their open contempt for authority with wary longing—the beat is envy of people who refuse to disappear.

chapters.title: A Letter Sealed in Wax
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The dying Colonel Ashworth, delirious with fever, presses a sealed letter into Marguerite's hands and whispers that it names 'the Zhus'—his own family—in a plot to divert an estate before the century turns. The beat is vertigo: the invisible man suddenly holds something everyone will want.

chapters.title: What the Dead Actually Named
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with a flashback to his father's disowned merchant years. He breaks the seal privately and finds the colonel's testament redirecting the Harrowgate inheritance to families erased from the official record—names that echo entries in his own ledger. The beat is recognition: two kinds of record-keeping are the same work.

chapters.title: Orders Come at Dawn
chapters.summary: Captain Reyes arrives to collect the colonel's effects, including 'any correspondence,' and Marguerite lies for the first time in his careful life. The beat is fear sharpening into resolve; he realizes the checkpoints were built for exactly this moment, and staying invisible was never really an option.

chapters.title: The Ferry That Isn't Licensed
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Marguerite approaches Ilsa about moving a parcel upriver before New Year's Eve. She refuses money but agrees when she reads one name from his ledger—a soldier she loved. The beat is the first crack in Marguerite's solitude: trust extended by someone with more to lose than he does.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, Counted
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He maps the route: the customs house at the bridge, the garrison gate at Millbrook, and the harbor fort at the river mouth, each requiring papers he cannot forge. The beat is cold planning as grief; he measures the journey in what can be carried, and the letter weighs nothing and everything.

chapters.title: Odile's Back Room
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The tavern widow shelters Marguerite overnight and reveals she has hidden fugitives for twenty years since her husband was erased from the same kind of ledger. The beat is solidarity across generations of the overlooked; she teaches him that belonging is practiced, not inherited.

chapters.title: The Girl from Page Forty
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He tracks down Nell, the orphaned daughter of Private Corrigan, whose name fills page forty of his ledger, intending only to deliver a promised letter. Instead he finds himself lying to authorities to keep her out of the workhouse. The beat is involuntary love—the found family assembling itself around him.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Disguised as a coal shipment, the letter passes the bridge customs house by minutes when an inspector recognizes Ilsa's revoked license and detains them. Marguerite talks his way through using his hospital credentials. The beat is adrenaline and its cost—he has spent his credibility and cannot pass this way twice.

chapters.title: Reyes Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Captain Reyes's POV. Reyes, himself complicit in the plot but increasingly uneasy, narrows the search to the harbor district and offers a reward that tempts even friends. The beat is menace from within: the antagonist is not a monster but a tired man following orders, which is worse.

chapters.title: Nell Learns the Ledger
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Hiding in the hospital cellar, Nell discovers the ledger and reads her father's entry aloud. Marguerite, caught, explains why he keeps it. The beat is tenderness under pressure; she asks to learn the names, and he begins teaching her—an apprenticeship in memory that mirrors his own inheritance.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Garrison Gate
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The Millbrook plan collapses when the garrison doubles its patrols after a tip. Ilsa proposes the suicidal alternative: running the millrace at night in fog. The beat is dread becoming commitment—each of them now chooses the risk rather than being chosen by it.

chapters.title: The Millrace at Night
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The night run nearly drowns them; the letter survives inside Marguerite's coat against his chest while he clings to the hull. They pass the garrison gate unseen. The beat is terror transfigured into intimacy—two people who trusted no one now bound by shared water and silence.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Tavern
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A paid informant among her regulars tips off Reyes; soldiers ransack the back room hours after Marguerite leaves. Odile is arrested. The beat is guilt and fury—Marguerite learns that his presence endangers everyone who shelters him, and that invisibility protected no one but himself all along.

chapters.title: The Price of Carrying
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He debates destroying the letter and fleeing with Nell, measuring escape against duty. Reading the colonel's testament again, he understands the names include Odile's late husband. The beat is moral crisis resolved into purpose: he will not trade one erasure for another.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Harbor Fort
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On New Year's Eve, with the fort gates sealed for the governor's ceremony, Marguerite walks openly toward the checkpoint carrying the letter in plain sight inside his ledger, betting that no one stops a nurse delivering records. The beat is audacity born of exhaustion—the invisible man makes himself unmistakable.

chapters.title: Stopped at the Gate
chapters.summary: Reyes's POV. Reyes intercepts him, alone, away from witnesses, and demands the letter. Marguerite instead opens the ledger and reads the names aloud—Corrigan, Brandt's soldier, Odile's husband—until Reyes, recognizing his own dead brother among them, lowers his pistol. The beat is the climax: testimony as weapon, and the antagonist's quiet defection.

chapters.title: Before the Century Turns
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. As midnight bells ring, the letter reaches the probate court through Reyes's sworn hand; the ceremony at the fort dissolves into rumor; Odile walks free. The beat is breathless release—the old century closes with its old order cracking along the seams the dead had already drawn.

chapters.title: What the Court Could Not Undo
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Weeks later, the estate transfers to the named families, though the officials who plotted it escape punishment. Marguerite rages at the partial justice until Nell points out that the ledger did what courts could not: it made the names undeniable. The beat is tempered hope—inheritance measured in memory, not money.

chapters.title: A Compass for the Harbor
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Ilsa regains her license ferrying harbor workers; Odile reopens the tavern with a new wall bearing the ledger's names in paint; Nell takes the stool beside Marguerite each evening to add new entries. The beat is belonging made daily practice—the compass of the title is the community itself, pointing home.

chapters.title: The First Name Written Freely
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, closing frame. On the anniversary of the colonel's death, Marguerite opens a fresh ledger and, for the first time, writes his own full name at the top of the first page—no longer omitted, no longer carried, but kept. The beat is quiet triumph: the man who measured the world in what can be carried finally sets it down among family.
